messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
TL;DR

Lorebooks act like REMINDERS to a bot.

When a KEYWORD is said, the bot gets reminded of the context behind that keyword.

That context stays in the memory for 4 messages.

ACTIVATION (you or bot)

Message 1
Message 2
Message 3
Message 4

DEACTIVATION (bot forgets context)

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
So say you list a character's name like JOHN SMITH as the KEYWORD, and the context for that name is

"Deceased"

When the name JOHN SMITH gets said, the bot is reminded "oh yeah, he's dead"

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content: That way the bot doesn't bring him back to life over and over again.

threads.title: Question About The Context And How It Takes Place With Lorebook And The Chatbot Itself

messages.author: PerFiLoRD
messages.content: Okay, I have a question. I am trying to optimise my own private bot and a lorebook, for more efficient usage of context space. And let's say, something is written in the "scenario" tab, for example, "{{char}} did X to {{user}}" and then, same thing, maybe worded differently, written in the lorebook, under char\user name tag will have written the same thing - will it take double space in the context, or only one of them will apply?

messages.author: Jake
messages.content:
> tag will have written the same thing - will it take double space in the context, or only one of them will apply?
It will take a double space inside the context. Whenever Lorebook entry is triggered, it injects itself into context without looking up if the same thing is already in the bot itself. It has it's minor uses in solidifying how the bot behaves, but generally it's a waste of space. What you can do, is describe something very briefly in the scenario, then do a more detailed description of said event in the Lorebook. This way, the bot always has some knowledge about the event, and when it comes to talk about it, the Lorebook triggers, providing more context.

threads.title: Explaining Memory Tokens And Other Stuff In Laymen S Terms For The Average Joe

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## Does having more memory help?
Having extra memory helps an AI stay in character, but only up to a point. If you overload it with too much backstory and chat history, its responses can actually get messier and less creative.

## How does the AI memory actually work?
An AI doesn't have a human brain that stores memories over time, because the AI does not understand the concept of time to begin with, as it cannot actually experience it.

It actually forgets everything the second it responds to you. When you type a new message, it will re-read your entire chat, plus any accessible information (such as the persona of your profile) from the beginning just to catch itself up.

**Working memory:** Think of this as the AI's reading capacity... the maximum amount of text it can scan in a single burst.

**Forgetting old details:** If the chat gets longer than its reading capacity, the system simply crops off the oldest messages. To the AI, those early events literally never happened. So if you have 8000 tokens and you then reach 9000 tokens, the first 1000 tokens are erased from memory.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## How does the AI know what to say next?
You can think of an AI as a super-smart (depending on your definition of smart, I mainly just see it as being able to recognize patterns) autocomplete.

Every time you send a message, it goes through three quick steps:

**Scans the room:** It reads the character profile, the setup rules, and whatever past messages fit into its reading limit.

**Plays the odds:** It looks at all that text and figures out which word(s) makes the most sense to type next.

**Focuses on details:** It tries to spotlight the specific words in your history that matter most to whatever is happening in the story right now. For example, if you're talking about your HOUSE and previous messages mention you leaving and entering your house over and over again, its gonna use that info as well.

## Does extra memory actually help?
Yup... but it is a balancing act.

**Why extra memory is great:** It stops the AI from suddenly forgetting main characters, past choices, or major plot points. It also gives you plenty of room to paste in detailed character backstories and rules.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## Does too much memory causes problems?
**It misses the middle:** The AI pays the closest attention to its original instructions and your very last message. Anything buried in the middle of a massive chat often gets overlooked.

**Character drift:** Over time, thousands of words of random chat history can drown out the character's original personality. It starts copying the general vibe of the recent chat instead of acting like the character you built.

**Getting distracted:** The AI tries to digest everything at once. If it rains in chapter one, it might assume it's still raining twenty chapters later because it struggles to tell old background details apart from what's happening right now.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## So what is the "sweet spot"?

**Too small (4K or less)**
Experience: Poor
Pros: Great for the first few messages or so if ya need a quick fix.
Cons: Constant amnesia. It forgets names, places, and what happened two turns ago.

**The sweet spot (16K)**
Experience: Solid/Best
Cons: Not great for long-term roleplay, as the memory quickly runs out when you spam tokens like you're shooting heroin.
Pros: Remembers key events while keeping the conversation sharp, fast, and creative (as long as you balance your token usage, how the bot and persona is worded).

**Too large (greater than 16K)**
Experience: Blurry/Inconclusive
Cons: The bot starts acting out of persona, repeating itself, or getting confused by old details. The bot has to re-read so much shit, it becomes a garbled clusterfuck.
Pros: Great for long-term roleplays (if you can ignore the constant confusion due to the bot having to re-read everything and guess what makes sense to say next).

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## In conclusion
More memory keeps the story on track, but with too much, it usually backfires. You get the best results by keeping the memory set to a balanced size and occasionally writing a quick summary of past events to keep the AI focused on the current scene.

Remember, the AI is a large language model, it doesn't understand spacial awareness, numbers, or context. It simply re-reads all the info and goes "uhhh, maybe this is the best answer to reply with?"

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## Why should you use lorebooks?

Have you ever had a doctor's appointment, then forgot about it?

Well, think of lorebooks like a collection of sticky notes or a reminder on your phone. When worded correctly, it re-informs the bot of some shit that is on a NEED TO KNOW basis when the bot NEEDS TO KNOW it.

For example... you don't always NEED TO KNOW and be thinking about your license plate number.

But you do NEED TO KNOW this for when you get pulled over.

Same idea with lorebooks, it takes information that you don't always NEED TO KNOW, and reminds the bot of that information when it is NEEDED.

Of course, keep in mind... the bot still has a token limit, and the bot is still going by the assumption that the MOST TALKED ABOUT THING is still more important than whatever the lorebook tells it.

However, the way you word a lorebook changes how the bot uses or interacts with the information.


Simply put, it checks the TRIGGER WORD / KEYWORD then uses that word to load the entry information every 2-4 messages when the word pops up.

The bot can trigger these itself.


For example:

ENTRY: John is dead.
This indeed tells the bot that JOHN IS DEAD, however, this doesn't tell the bot whether or not it KNOWS that JOHN IS DEAD. So odds are, the bot is gonna go "uhhh, should I respond to this or nah?"

ENTRY: {{char}} knows John is dead.
Same as above, but ENFORCES the idea that the character KNOWS this, and therefore is more likely to use this context to inform its newest response.

Additionally, if the post that triggers the entry has no reason to reference the entry, it will often go unused.

Such as mentioning that you "like John's soup". Any normal conversation wouldn't then be like "by the way, John died".

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## What else can I do with a lorebook?

You can use it to ENFORCE commands or behaviors.


For example...

ENTRY: {{char}} hates {{user}}
So whenever the trigger word appears, it informs the bot that its newest response is in the context of the character HATING the {{user}}.

ENTRY: {{char}} values honesty
Same as with above, this ENFORCES the idea that HONESTY is a value for the character, and therefore will try to reinforce this belief in upcoming responses or reactions to what the {{user}} says.

ENTRY: {{char}} will stop speaking for the {{user}}
Once again, it REINFORCES the command of saying "hey chatbot, stop talking for me".


Remember, HOW you word it can make all the difference.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## What is "Temperature" for in AI model settings?

**Temperature: The "Creativity Dial"**
This controls how wild or predictable the bot's mood is.

**Low setting (0.0 – 0.5):** *The Serious Assistant.* It plays it totally safe, sticking to logical, straightforward words. It is consistent and accurate, but can sound a bit boring.
**High setting (0.8 – 1.5):** *The Wild Storyteller.* It takes big risks, choosing surprising or creative words. It is great for brainstorming, but if you turn it up too high, it might start talking non-sense.
**Default:** 0.7 (A nice balance of logical and interesting).

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## What the fuck does Top-P and Top-K do?

**Top-P: The "Word Pool Filter"**
Before the bot speaks, it creates a list of reasonable word choices and ranks them by probability. Top-P cuts off the bottom percentage of unlikely choices.

**Low setting (0.01 – 0.5):** *The Strict Filter.* It throws out almost all risky options and only lets the bot pick from the absolute safest, most obvious words.
**High setting (0.8 – 1.0):** *The Open Door.* It keeps almost all word options on the table, allowing rare or unique phrases to slip through.
**Default:** 0.7 (It considers the top 70% of sensible options and ignores the bottom 30% of weird ones).

**Top-K: The "Vocabulary Limit"**
Instead of using percentages like Top-P, Top-K sets a strict, hard limit on the exact *number* of word options the bot is allowed to look at for its next choice.

**Low setting (1 – 20):** *Tiny Vocabulary.* The bot can only choose from a tiny handful of the most common words (e.g., forcing it to pick only from its top 5 options). It will never make a mistake, but it will sound repetitive.
**High setting (50 – 100):** *Huge Vocabulary.* The bot can scan through 90+ possible words for every single choice, giving it tons of variety—though occasionally it might pick an odd word that sounds out of place.
**Default:** 90 (It looks at up to 90 word choices at a time).

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## Rough estimate of token limits per tier

Let's assume you're talking to a 500 token bot.

Each post a bot makes, generally takes up between 120 to 240 tokens. (Halve your reply options if your posts also take up between 120 to 240 tokens)

Let's also assume your persona is empty.

At best, each subscription will get...

FREE: 2400 tokens (7+ replies)
GET A TASTE: 4000 tokens (14+ replies)
TRUE SUPPORTER: 8000 tokens (31+ replies)
ALL-IN: 16000 tokens (64+ replies)

...before your context memory runs out.

This is not including things like memory manager, lorebooks, group chats, etc.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## Understanding how language works for LLMs

1. Avoid using words and phrases like "do not" and "never".
Instead, use stronger reinforcement words, such as "prohibit" or "restrict". LLMs understand these words and often follow them to a much higher degree.

2. Avoid using unnecessary words.
You don't need to say "ancient medieval town", simply "medieval town" implies that it is ancient. LLMs understand the nuance of words, and use these words to enforce a greater understanding of the world or information. For example, if you say "cyberpunk world", the bot will automatically assume that it contains "high tech", "corrupted governments/corporations", and other similar things.

3. There is no right way to make a bot.
Whether using plain text, script, or compacted, each way you organize it, what words you use, and what rules or guidelines you enforce, can completely change how the bot reacts. Additionally, how the {{user}} responds, what their persona information says, what AI model is used, and what temperature and top-P/top-K settings are used completely change every experience, so there is no "best for everyone" or "universal" way to make a bot that everyone can enjoy.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
## UNDERSTANDING CONTEXT WINDOW vs TOTAL MEMORY

Chatbots do not actually have a brain or a long-term human memory. Instead, they rely on a fixed "short-term memory" frame called a context window, which acts like a scrolling whiteboard of text.

***What is a Context Window?***

Imagine the bot is sitting at a desk with a small whiteboard. Every time you send a message, the app writes down your message *and* the bot's past replies on that whiteboard.

**The Catch:** The whiteboard has a fixed size (measured in "tokens," or roughly word chunks).
**The Illusion:** When you send a new message, the AI isn't "remembering" your previous conversation. It is reading the entire whiteboard from top to bottom all over again to figure out what to say next.

***Why Chatbots Seem to "Forget" Everything***

If it feels like the bot suddenly loses track of details after a few exchanges, it is usually due to three main mechanics:

**The Whiteboard Fills Up (The Sliding Window):** Once the conversation gets too long, the app has to erase the top lines of the whiteboard to make room for your newest message. Anything erased instantly ceases to exist for the AI.
**The "Lost in the Middle" Effect:** Even within a large context window, AI models pay the most attention to the very beginning (system rules) and the very end (your latest prompt). Details buried in the middle of a long conversation get blurry or ignored.


***A Partial Fix***
To save space, summarizing the conversation so far (all the memory) into your memory manager helps the bot maintain some ability to remain coherent a little bit longer.
